content: The global burden of viral infections caused by unsafe medical injections was analyzed between 2000 and 2010, with findings published in PLoS One in 2014. The study highlighted the need for safer medical practices to reduce the transmission of infections. Additionally, the World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines in 2014 on the safe management of healthcare waste, emphasizing the importance of proper disposal methods to prevent environmental contamination and disease spread. Efforts to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare facilities, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, have been shown to reduce healthcare-associated infections. A 2018 report by the National Institute for Health Research reviewed interventions aimed at enhancing drinking water quality, sanitation, and handwashing facilities in healthcare settings. These interventions are critical for improving patient safety and reducing infection risks. The WHO and UNICEF have collaborated on global strategies to address the burden of disease and prioritize actions for improving WASH in healthcare facilities. Reports from workshops and global learning events, such as those held in London (2016) and Kathmandu (2017), have provided actionable solutions and shared best practices for implementing WASH improvements. The UN-Water Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-Water (GLAAS) 2017 report highlighted the status of WASH services worldwide, emphasizing the need for sustained investments and policy implementation to achieve universal access to safe water and sanitation. The WHO and UNICEF also published a 2015 report on the current status of WASH in healthcare facilities, outlining a roadmap for future improvements. International agreements, such as the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (2004) and the Basel Convention on Hazardous Waste (1989), have established frameworks for managing environmental health risks. These conventions underscore the importance of addressing hazardous waste in healthcare settings to protect public health and the environment. Cost analyses, such as a 2017 study on portable handwashing and drinking water stations in rural Kenyan healthcare facilities, have demonstrated the economic feasibility and health benefits of WASH interventions. These findings support the integration of WASH improvements into broader healthcare quality initiatives. The WHO has developed tools and guidelines to support WASH improvements in healthcare facilities. For example, the Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) provides a risk-based approach to assess, prioritize, and implement WASH improvements. Since its inception in 2015, WASH FIT has been implemented in over 20 countries, demonstrating its adaptability and effectiveness in diverse settings. Infection prevention and control (IPC) programs are essential for reducing healthcare-associated infections and combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The WHO emphasizes the integration of WASH and IPC programs at both national and facility levels to enhance patient safety and healthcare quality. Universal health coverage (UHC) cannot be achieved without adequate WASH services. Access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene is fundamental to delivering quality healthcare and achieving desired health outcomes. The WHO and UNICEF have developed global indicators to monitor progress on WASH in healthcare facilities, aligning with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The WHO's guidelines on drinking water quality, sanitation, and infection prevention provide a comprehensive framework for improving environmental health standards in healthcare settings. These guidelines are complemented by tools such as the Infection Prevention and Control Assessment Framework (IPCAF) and the Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, which support countries in implementing effective WASH and IPC strategies. Regional initiatives, such as those in Africa, Southeast Asia, and Europe, have integrated WASH standards into broader healthcare quality and emergency response strategies. For example, Serbia has improved WASH surveillance in healthcare facilities by incorporating global indicators into its national monitoring program. This approach has led to targeted improvements in rural and primary healthcare settings, addressing gaps in sanitation and hygiene. The WHO and UNICEF continue to advocate for WASH improvements in healthcare facilities through global monitoring, policy development, and capacity-building efforts.
